title: Where I Stand
description: A quiet reflection on uncertainty, reinvention and what it means to begin again while standing between identities, countries and chapters.
bodyHtml:
A quiet reflection on uncertainty, reinvention, and what it means to begin again.

A husband. A father. Packed up a life, chased a new one across oceans and time zones, with nothing but belief folded between documents and dreams. And paperwork that doesn’t always move with your plans.

I’m in the middle of an MBA. They call it executive. But sometimes, it feels like it’s executing me. Let’s just say the winds aren’t exactly gentle right now.

There’s too much riding on this chapter, And I wonder: Am I chasing success, or just outrunning fear?

And then, on a bench, in the calm between two storms, a friend sits beside me. Looks me in the eye. Doesn’t ask. Doesn’t fix. Just says:

“Let me tell you a story. It’s mine. But maybe, just maybe, you’ll see yourself in it.”

And so it begins. A memory. A mirror. One story at a time.

About this series: This is the first entry of a storytelling series. It isn’t advice. It isn’t a playbook. It’s just a life, told in pieces, sometimes messy, sometimes meaningful.

If any part of it resonates with you, I invite you to follow along.

title: Gratitude
subtitle: Not for something new, but for what has always been there.
description: A reflection on family, distance and learning to notice what matters before it disappears.
bodyHtml:
“Man, I’m in a bit of a mess,” I told Bobby the other day.

“Family in one place, work in another. EMBA classes. Career thoughts. It’s like I’m living five lives at once and barely keeping up with one.”

Bobby paused. Then smiled.

“I hear you. Sounds like one of those sticky, heavy seasons. But before we even start untangling anything… can I say something? Be grateful. Not later—now. You’ve already got more than you think.”

I was quiet.

He leaned in and said, “Look at your life. You’ve got a daughter who looks for you. A partner who believes in you. A home. A path. A story that’s still unfolding. And you come from people who shaped you. That’s rare, man. You’re already standing on gold.”

And just like that, something shifted in me.

I was born and brought up in a joint family—fifteen of us under one roof.

It was loud, chaotic, and full of love. We didn’t have a lot. But we had each other. Every day was shared meals, space, silence, noise and stories. Back then, it didn’t feel like anything special. It was just… life.

Then I moved. For work. For marriage. For responsibility. And slowly, the phone calls became fewer. The visits, rare. That warm, messy chaos faded.

Now I live in a quieter home, in a different country. And I’ve realised I miss the noise.

I miss the unsolicited advice. The nagging. The late-night chai. The crowded sofa. The background hum of people who loved you in their own flawed, beautiful way.

I didn’t leave because I wanted to. I left because I had to. But a part of me is still there on that verandah, barefoot, listening to stories I didn’t understand at the time.

And here’s what I’ve learned:

We spend so much time chasing what’s next. But most of us already have what matters.

A roof. Food. Someone who cares. Even just a moment of peace. So many in the world don’t even have that.

Gratitude isn’t about counting blessings. It’s about noticing them before they disappear. It’s not about saying thank you when everything is perfect. It’s about realising that right here, right now, you are already standing in the middle of something good.

So today, I’m pausing. To say thanks. To where I come from. And to everything I still carry from that home, even when I’m far from it.

title: I Wasn’t Sure I’d Last a Month
description: A story about arriving in Singapore with doubt, slowly finding belonging and discovering that surviving can itself be a form of strength.
bodyHtml:
Bobby and I were still talking after our gratitude chat. I had just finished a little rant about how unsure I’ve been feeling lately.

He smiled and said,

“Okay. But what about your strengths?”

I laughed.

“Strengths? Right now, I feel like I’m just surviving.”

“Exactly,” he said. “And that’s a strength too.”

That took me back to 2012. To a quiet, warm morning in Singapore, my first day.

I had landed the night before. Told myself I was doing this to be closer to someone incredibly special…

that’s a series of its own, full of ups and downs, impossible choices, quiet pain, joy, tears, and even a phase where I seriously considered leaving it all behind. Monkhood wasn’t just a metaphor, it felt real at the time. One day, that story will have a chapter of its own.

Back to Singapore, truthfully, I was starting from scratch, with no idea if I’d make it.

That morning, I stepped out for a short walk.

Everything around me was new. The streets, the signs, the people. I had stepped into a place where I was a foreigner not just in nationality, but in culture, in rhythm.

Back home, I knew how things worked. Here, I was starting from zero. I didn’t have a network. I didn’t fully understand the business landscape. May be it was fear of the unknown...

And honestly, I didn’t know if I could.

“I don’t think I’ll last more than a month,” I remember telling myself.

But I stayed.

And slowly, without even realizing it, I began to grow. Not just in my work, but in the way I saw the world.

Over time, I had the chance to contribute to something meaningful. We grew the business across Southeast Asia. Expanded teams, opened remote offices, explored new ideas. But more than any numbers, it was the relationships, the trust, and the learning that shaped me.

Singapore didn’t just give me a job. It gave me a space to become more.

I don’t know when exactly it happened, but by the time I left 12 years later, Singapore had become home.

It taught me patience. It taught me how belonging doesn’t happen overnight, it’s built, one moment at a time. And it taught me how much richer life becomes when you embrace difference, not with fear, but with curiosity.

Even now, the thought of going back always lingers.

And if that version of me, the one walking around on Day 1, could see me now, I think he’d say:

“Keep showing up, even when you’re unsure. Stay curious, work with heart, and welcome what’s unfamiliar. Be real with people. Be honest with yourself. And always give your best.”

Maybe Bobby was right.

Sometimes surviving is a strength, Not because it looks impressive from the outside, But because you stayed in it long enough to grow.

title: Finding My Voice
subtitle: When survival turns into self-awareness.
description: A sixth-grade language struggle became an early lesson in originality, effort and the value of trusting my own voice.
bodyHtml:
Bobby and I were sitting outside after a long day, still talking about what it means to survive.

I brought up that old frog story.

“You know, the one where the frog sits in a bowl of water?” I said.

“The heat goes up slowly, and it just keeps adjusting. Until the water starts boiling… and it’s too late.”

Bobby nodded.

“It’s important to hear your own voice and be aware of the space you’re in—what they call self-awareness.”

His words took me back to sixth grade.

Until fifth grade, life was familiar. Telugu was my mother tongue.

Then came a new school, and my second language was now Hindi—a language I had never read before.

My first exam felt like staring at a wall of symbols I couldn’t decode.

When the marks came back, red ink cut across the page. I had failed. Badly.

I still remember that moment: standing in the staff room, holding the marksheet, and for the first time in my life, crying out loud.

Not quietly. Not holding back. Just a raw, unfiltered reaction.

In that moment, I was the frog in the warming water, realising the heat was rising faster than I could adjust.

So I started from square one.

Letter by letter. Word by word.

My grammar was poor, my spelling worse—but I kept grinding.

Then came the midterms.

One question was open-ended: “What do you think?”

I didn’t have perfect words, so I used the ones I had.

Mistakes aside, it was honest. It was mine.

When the results came, something unexpected happened.

The class topper—the one who never lost marks—had dropped points in that section. Curious, he read my paper.

“Wait… you scored more than me here?”

Turns out, I had.

Not for flawless grammar, but for originality. For honesty. For effort.

That was my shift—the moment survival became awareness.

I realised my voice mattered, even in a language I barely knew.

And once you see that, you can’t go back to just staying afloat.

I looked at Bobby and said, “Maybe strength is knowing when survival has quietly turned into self-awareness—and you start seeing yourself differently.”

title: Winners Do Things Differently
description: What repeated exposure to high-performing people revealed about discipline, preparation and the small choices behind visible success.
bodyHtml:
Last week, Bobby and I were talking about confidence. Not the loud kind. But the kind that shows up slowly when you’ve survived long enough to grow. When you've become aware of your own strength, even in silence.

This week, we took that thought a step further.

“So… once you’ve found confidence,” Bobby asked, “What do you do with it?”

I paused. Because that’s when courage enters the picture.

Confidence makes you feel ready. Courage is what moves your feet.

And that took me back to a chapter from my early career in India.

It was early in my career in India. We were a strong team, respected, consistent, and well-known across the company. But every year, during the annual sales ceremony, where the top-performing offices were honored, we found ourselves clapping for others. Always close. Never called.

We had the talent. The trust. The reputation. But the stage? It remained out of reach.

Then came a shift, a niche product line that no one was paying attention to. Low visibility. Low expectations. Low interest. But my manager saw something others didn’t.

“What if we co-promoted this product with a major MNC?”

It had never been done before. It was risky. Different. Easy to dismiss. But he believed in it. And more importantly, he believed in us.

That belief sparked courage.

We stepped into unfamiliar territory and stayed there for nearly two years. And along the way, we met resistance, doubt, and fatigue.

Initial outreach was discouraging. Customers were polite, but hesitant. It felt like we were pushing uphill, alone. We didn’t give up. We took it one client at a time.

The first few conversions came in. Small, yes but they gave us momentum. It wasn’t validation. But it was hope.

Some questioned the focus: “Why invest so much in something unproven?” We didn’t argue. We just kept building.

Momentum picked up. Clients began to see value. Word spread. Resistance faded.

As we approached the end of the second year, things weren’t looking the way we had hoped. Despite all our effort, the revenue from this experiment was only trickling in not flooding.

There were whispers. Was this worth it? Had we overestimated the opportunity?

After two years of work, this hit hard. Because it wasn’t just a project on the line.

The long hours, the risks, the belief we’d poured into this,suddenly felt fragile.

Eventually, we crossed a major threshold, We had shifted over 50% of the segment in our favor.

That year, we became the top-selling business unit in India for that product line. I was named the Best Salesperson nationwide.

But honestly, it wasn’t about the title. Or the numbers.

For our team, the real win came the night of the annual sales ceremony.

After years of sitting in the audience, applauding others... We finally heard our office name called. We finally stood on that stage, together.

Not because we followed the norm. But because we dared to do something different, and had the courage to stay with it long enough to prove it mattered.

“So… was that your boldest move?” Bobby asked me not long ago. I smiled. “No. The boldest part wasn’t the idea. It was showing up every day, long before anyone else believed it would work.”

He nodded.

“That’s the thing about courage,” he said. “It doesn’t always feel brave. Sometimes… it just feels right.”

title: A Trip Down Memory Lane
description: Looking back at the people, places and moments that quietly shape who we become, even when we do not recognise their influence at the time.
bodyHtml:
Today is Vinayaka Chavithi, a festival very close to my heart.

In Indian tradition, Lord Vinayaka (Ganesha) is the first among gods. No auspicious work begins without invoking him. His life stories carry wisdom and management lessons, and I’m sure LinkedIn will be full of those today.

But instead of retelling myths, I want to share my own story, how we celebrated when I was a child. And maybe, years later, my daughter (who, after reading my earlier posts, told me I need to “check my grammar, commas, and full stops!” 😅) will know how her father grew up.

Morning Rituals in a Joint Family

In a joint family, even “getting ready” is an event.

By 5 a.m., my grandmother would already be boiling water in a giant pot over firewood. I loved sitting near the flames, feeding sticks into the fire, the warmth slowly shaking off my sleep.

Then came the oil bath ritual. A line of kids, waiting their turn, while my grandmother lovingly massaged us from head to toe with oil. Eyes stinging, bodies sticky and then came her secret weapon: shikakai.

Now, shikakai wasn’t just picked up at a store. My grandmother prepared it herself, drying shikakkai pods along with amla, hibiscus, fenugreek seeds, and a few other herbs out in the sun. Once perfectly crisp, she would take them to the local grinding mill, where they’d be turned into a fine brown powder. This wasn’t just shampoo. It was shampoo + soap + conditioner + scrub all rolled into one natural powder.

Basically, the “all-in-one body wash” of its time… except it burned your eyes and left you squeaky clean whether you liked it or not. Think of it as the original 4-in-1 product, no fancy bottle, no ads, just your grandma making sure you didn’t escape!

The fragrance lingered with me the whole day. Even now, when I think of Vinayaka Chaturthi, I first smell shikakai.

Dressing Up & The Market Walk

After the bath, my father or grandfather helped me wear my dhoti, carefully folding and tucking it in place. Then came the highlight of the morning: the trip to the market with my Uncle VJ.

The lanes were narrow but full of life, vendors under small tarpaulin sheets, each selling clay idols, flowers, fruits, sugarcane, banana plants, mango leaves. Some stalls tried to cover everything, but most were humble, just daily vendors trying to make ends meet, hoping the festival rush gave them enough for the day.

The most fascinating part for me was watching clay idols being pressed into molds right there on the street. Their hands moved with rhythm and speed, transforming clay into gods, felt almost magcal to watch.

And then, of course, choosing the umbrella for the idol. Every year new designs appeared, and as kids we argued over which one looked the best. Carrying the idol home in baskets felt like the proudest responsibility.

Prayers, Food & Quiet Love

Back home, my grandfather would lead the prayers. Kids always got the front row, elders sat behind us. While the rituals went on, my grandmother, mother, and aunts worked tirelessly in the kitchen.

Vinayaka is said to love kudumulu (steamed dumplings with coconut-jaggery filling). Honestly, I don’t know if Vinayaka loves them, but I sure did.

When the prayers ended, we all sat cross-legged on the floor in rows, eating from banana leaves. This wasn’t just about food, sitting down together, batch after batch, the kind that bonded us without words.

I usually ate fast, not to run off, but because I loved cleaning the floor for the next round and serving food to others. In a joint family, love wasn’t often spoken out loud. It was shown, in serving, in cleaning, in making sure the next person was cared for. That was my way of saying “I love you.”

We ended with paan, betel leaf folded with slacked lime and betel nut.

The Community Spirit

By afternoon, once the feast was over, our cycles were ready. This was our time. No phones, no watches, just a pack of kids riding through narrow lanes, each street buzzing with its own celebrations.

Every neighborhood had set up its own Vinayaka idol, often crafted with creativity and pride. Some were simple clay idols decorated with fresh flowers, while others were more elaborate painted in bright colors, holding little props, sometimes even themed to reflect a social message. For us kids, it was like a festival treasure hunt, who had the biggest idol, the funniest decoration, or the most colorful umbrella.

Chennai, where I grew up, kept the celebrations modest. But whenever I visited Hyderabad, the difference was striking. Idols were massive, sometimes towering over buildings, with drums, music, and processions filling the air. The most iconic of them all, the Khairatabad Ganesh once stood at nearly 50 feet tall. Watching such giants slowly being carried for immersion on the 10th day, surrounded by thousands of people chanting and dancing, was an experience etched into my memory forever.

For us kids, though, the joy wasn’t just in the grandeur. It was in the freedom of the cycle rides, the laughter with friends, and the shared awe of discovering each idol, as if every street was telling its own story of devotion.

Carrying It Forward

Last year, my daughter Pia gave a presentation to her classmates about Vinayaka Chavithi. She spoke about the stories, the rituals, and the joy I once knew as a child. And just like my grandmother and mother did for me, her mom, this time to make dozens of kolukattai (sweet dumplings) as a treat for Pia’s friends.

Needless to say, her classmates loved both the stories and the food. It felt special to see how these traditions, once rooted in firewood baths and banana-leaf feasts, now found their way into a classroom in California, the same festival, just told in a new voice.

Looking Back

As a child, I didn’t see the invisible labor, my grandmother drying shikakkai, my aunts cooking for hours, my parents making sure everything ran smoothly. Today, I see it as love.

When I think about it now, festivals were never just about rituals or offerings. To me, they were occasions to gather as a family, celebrate together, and spread joy. The rituals themselves almost seemed designed to bring people closer, sitting in rows to eat, serving each other food, visiting neighbors, and sharing stories.

Perhaps that was always the deeper purpose: creating a sense of togetherness, a reminder that joy multiplies when it is shared.

title: Second Chances and First Choices
description: A reflection on regret, agency and the difference between being given another opportunity and choosing differently when it arrives.
bodyHtml:
I learned the answer years ago, when dishonesty cost me something far greater than a job, it cost me peace of mind.

The Question That Started It

Just last week, a friend in school asked me: “What’s a complete no-no for you?” Without hesitation, I said: dishonesty.

They looked surprised. Almost as if to say, that’s a low bar.

But for me, honesty isn’t a lofty ideal. It’s the foundation. Without it, everything else collapses.

That evening, I came home and put on a movie. Its theme? Honesty. Redemption. Life giving you a second chance to do the right thing.

It felt like more than coincidence. A reminder. And it pulled me back to one of the most difficult lessons of my life.

Early Career Crossroads

After graduation in India, life was simple but intense. I was part of a close group of seven friends, all of us chasing jobs. One by one, each friend got placed. Soon, only two of us were left me and one close friend, still searching, still hopeful.

The air was filled with competition. But for us, it was also about camaraderie. We were in this together.

A Decision I Regret

And then came the interruption, the test not of my skills, but of my values.

I came across a job posting at Bosch. A big opportunity. I applied. But I didn’t tell my friend.

Why? Somewhere in me, I thought his chance meant less of mine. It was a small decision, but it shifted something inside.

Lessons in Vulnerability

When I got shortlisted, I felt a rush of excitement. I traveled to another city for the test and interview, telling myself this was my chance.

But guilt traveled with me. On the train, in the exam hall, even as I sat across from the interviewer, I kept hearing the same voice: “You should have told him.”

I flunked the interview. And oddly, I felt relief. Not because of the failure, but because deep down I knew I hadn’t earned it.

When I returned, the guilt didn’t let go. I went to my friend’s house, confessed everything, and apologized, bracing for disappointment.

The Treasure of Transparency

To my surprise, he smiled and said, “Don’t worry, I wasn’t even interested in that field.”

For him, it was nothing. For me, it was everything.

That day, I realized honesty isn’t about whether others are hurt, it’s about whether you can live with yourself.

Life didn’t give me the job. But it gave me something greater: a second chance to choose honesty.

Fast forward to now, back in school again: I no longer see classmates as competition. I see them as fellow travelers, each carrying something I can learn from. And if I don’t succeed, it isn’t because someone else got ahead, it simply means I still have more growing to do.

That experience taught me something simple: keeping things to myself doesn’t serve me, and it doesn’t serve others. So now, when I have access to information or resources, I share them. Because the real win isn’t when one of us succeeds, it’s when all of us grow together.

The treasure I carry is simple: second chances only exist to remind us to make better first choices.

title: Developing a Taste for Diversity
description: A personal reflection on food, familiarity and how openness to difference is often built gradually through ordinary experiences.
bodyHtml:
Last week, as Kerala (a southern state in India) celebrated Onam, I was reminded of how true that is.

Onam is Kerala’s biggest festival, marking the annual return of King Mahabali, a legendary ruler remembered for prosperity, equality, and kindness. For Keralites, Onam is not just about his homecoming, it is about reliving an ideal time when everyone was treated equally, and no one was left behind.

I grew up in a Telugu-speaking family but was raised in Chennai, a Tamil-speaking state. Even within South India alone (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, and Telangana), languages, cuisines, and traditions shift dramatically.

India’s diversity is staggering: 28 states, 22 official languages with their own scripts, and hundreds of dialects. My favorite way to explain it is simple: “In India, every 100 miles, the culture, language, cuisine, terrain, and even climate changes.”

When I started working in India, I was traveling 4/5 days a week. Until then, I had only read about this diversity. But travel gave me an opportunity to experience it. Crossing into a new state sometimes felt like crossing a national border, suddenly the food, greetings, and even the way people smiled were different.

That experience quietly trained me to adapt. Years later, when I moved to Singapore and then to the U.S., I realized how much this early exposure helped me embrace new environments.

Food as a Teacher

For over 20 years, I ate the same kind of food almost every day. I didn’t just have a comfort zone, I lived in it.

Then I got married. My wife has always been curious about cuisines. She dragged me into restaurants I never would have stepped into, encouraged me, sometimes forced me, to try new dishes.

Her line still echoes in my head: “You need to develop a taste for it.”

At the time, it was about food. Looking back, I realize it’s also about people and cultures. Sometimes you need to give yourself patience and openness to “develop a taste for it.” And once you do, you often end up loving it.

The Festive Heartbeat of India

Here’s the beauty of India: right from Onam in August–September, the festive season begins and doesn’t stop.

Every month, in some culture, somewhere in the country, a festival lights up homes, streets, and hearts, from Durga Puja and Diwali in the north, to Navratri and Pongal in the south, to countless local celebrations in between. Festivals become both a cultural heartbeat and an economic driver.

Back to Onam

It is not just a festival, it is the festival in Kerala.

Streets come alive with Pookalam, intricate flower carpets laid at the entrance of homes. Marigold, chrysanthemum, and jasmine are arranged petal by petal into bright mandalas, their fragrance mixing with the scent of coconut oil lamps.

For businesses, Onam is also peak season in Kerala. Retail stores put out their best offers of the year, and families shop in preparation for the festival. But cross into Tamil Nadu or Andhra Pradesh, and it’s the opposite, this is considered an inauspicious month, and sales slow down.

When I worked in the FMCD industry, this contrast struck me. The same month could mean booming demand in one state and a dry spell in another. It taught me that marketing in India is never “one size fits all.” Campaigns had to be designed with sensitivity to culture, festivals, and habits.

My Favorite Part: The Sadhya

Imagine sitting in front of a fresh green banana leaf, as dish after dish is placed before you, twenty or more in total.

The creamy Avial, a medley of vegetables in coconut and yogurt. The surprising burst of pineapple pachadi, sweet, tangy, and spiced. The crunch of pappadam, the tang of pulissery, the comfort of sambar.

And then the desserts. Not one, not two, but three different payasams, The jaggery-rich Ada Pradhaman, The silky Palada anf my personal weakness, the simple, comforting Semiya payasam

I’ll admit it: I have a sweet tooth. By the end of the feast, I’m not just eating dessert, I’m surrendering to it.

Even in Singapore, my wife and I would wait in line, sometimes 30 minutes, sometimes an hour, at a Kerala restaurant every Onam, just to enjoy this tradition. This reminds me that traditions are not bound by geography. They travel, adapt, and find new life in every corner of the world.

Self Reflection

And just like I developed a taste for new cuisines, I’ve also developed a taste for diversity. Thanks to my wife, it started at the dining table. Today, it extends to how I see the world.

Perhaps that is the real gift of festivals is that, they remind us that joy multiplies when we open ourselves to what is different, and that life becomes richer when we learn to celebrate each other’s traditions as our own.

👉 Over to you: What festival or tradition from your culture has shaped the way you see the world?

title: Listening My Way Forward
description: How hosting conversations helped an introvert discover that listening can be not only a strength, but also a way of leading.
bodyHtml:
If you had told me a year ago I’d be hosting a podcast, I would have laughed. As an introvert, I’ve always found it easier to listen than to step into the spotlight. But one of the biggest lessons from my UCLA EMBA journey is that growth often comes when we lean into connections, the kind that truly stretch us.

As one classmate put it beautifully in our conversation, this program also gives you the confidence to open doors, explore new skills, and see business from every angle. That line has stayed with me, because it captures exactly what this journey feels like.

Of course, the professors and academics are world-class, and they are a big reason we chose UCLA. But what I have tried to capture through my podcast, 5% Conversations, are the lessons that come from outside the classroom. The podcast has simply been a chance to sit down with classmates, listen to their journeys, and realize how much we can all learn from one another.

What started as an experiment has turned into one of my favorite classrooms. And what has been most heartening is how often the conversations return to the same theme, the cohort. Again and again, classmates spoke about how this community has been the real gift of the program, the friendships, the generosity, and the support that make an already demanding journey not just possible but memorable.

Yes, the academics are intense, more than most of us expected. The quarters move fast, the workload is heavy, and everyone is balancing careers, families, and school at the same time. I have heard about color-coded calendars, strict routines, and daily practices that keep people grounded. Time management here is not a theory, it is survival, and it teaches discipline in ways few other experiences can.

The diversity of stories has been striking. A walk among the sequoias turning into a reflection on resilience, how growth often comes through fire. The courage it takes to pause a career to care for family, reminding me that sometimes stepping back is the bravest move forward. Simple habits, like making the bed each morning, becoming anchors for bigger wins. Practical wisdom, like keeping two phones to draw clear boundaries. Stories of volunteering and service as a way to stay grounded. The grit behind filling stadiums, and the persistence required to bring a film from script to screen.

Different industries. Different journeys. And yet, the same themes echo through them all: resilience, balance, purpose.

What makes these lessons powerful is not that they come from textbooks, but that they come from classmates living them every day while navigating the same demanding program. That is what makes UCLA Anderson School of Management EMBA special. The faculty teach us frameworks and strategy, but the cohort teaches us how those lessons play out in real life. Together, they form a classroom richer than either could be alone.

I do not know where this podcast journey will lead, but I already know it has given me something invaluable: the reminder that listening is one of the most powerful ways to learn. And that sometimes the most important teachers are the people sitting right next to us.

Before I close, I want to say a heartfelt thank you to everyone who has joined me on 5% Conversations so far. Your openness, reflections, and generosity have made each conversation richer than I could have imagined. This little project only works because of the stories you have shared.

I also want to acknowledge the friends, families, and partners who stand behind us. They are the ones who quietly take on extra responsibilities, make sacrifices, and give us the space to grow. Without their support, none of this would be possible, and they are just as much a part of this journey as we are.

And this is just the beginning, If the first few episodes have taught me anything, it is that the best stories are still ahead.

title: Authenticity Doesn’t Shout
description: A reflection on the quieter signals of authenticity and why being genuine is often felt long before it is announced.
bodyHtml:
I read a piece in The Guardian about Taylor Swift’s latest album. Some praised it as her most honest work yet, while others called it over curated and less authentic. Around the same time, in one of my UCLA classes, a classmate mentioned how being authentic is harder than it sounds, especially when you are constantly adapting to new environments and expectations.

It made me pause and think. Because authenticity is not something we declare. It is something we live, often quietly. And I learned that lesson early, not in a boardroom or classroom, but on a school stage.

Finding My Voice

In my old school, I was active and expressive, part of every radio skit, every drama, every opportunity to perform. I simply enjoyed creating something with others. The stage was home. Teachers encouraged me. Friends recognized me. I did not think about being authentic. I just was.

Then life shifted. I moved to a new school. New language. New people. New rhythm. Everything felt unfamiliar. The students already had their circles. The teachers expected polished English. The boy who once felt comfortable in the spotlight became quiet in the back row.

When auditions were announced for an interschool skit, I saw it as a small chance to reconnect with who I used to be. I did not go in expecting much, only to participate and to belong.

During early rehearsals, I stumbled. My English was not strong enough for the lead part. My confidence cracked, and without much discussion, I was quietly moved to a background role.

It hurt more than I wanted to admit. But I stayed. I learned everyone’s lines, helped others rehearse, fixed cues, and made sure the play was ready. Even if I was not seen, I wanted the team to succeed.

That was when I began to understand something I had never realized before. Sometimes authenticity is not about standing out. Sometimes it is about quietly standing firm.

The Switch

Rehearsals went on for weeks. I worked behind the curtain, invisible but involved. There were nights I walked home wondering if it even mattered. Maybe I was meant to stay in the background.

And then, without warning, everything changed. A few days before the performance, our teacher announced a switch. I would now take the lead role.

I did not panic or celebrate. I just stepped in and did what I had been preparing for all along.

The play went smoothly. I went home relieved that it was over. The next morning, during assembly, my name was called. I had been awarded Best Actor.

That moment was not about winning. It was about belonging again.

The Quiet Reward

Looking back, the real reward was not the recognition. It was the belief I rediscovered.

When you keep showing up with honesty, when you contribute without seeking credit, your work eventually speaks for you.

Authenticity does not shout. It shows up quietly, in how you treat people, how you stay committed, and how you carry yourself when no one is watching.

That lesson has stayed with me ever since. Whether I am managing clients, working across teams, or building new ideas, I try to bring that same calm and steady energy. I do not chase visibility. I focus on adding value. I help others succeed. And when the time comes, I am ready to lead, not because I practiced being seen, but because I never stopped showing up.

Even in silence, authenticity has a voice.

title: Growing Together
description: Parenting is not only about helping a child grow. It also requires parents to keep changing, listening and learning alongside them.
bodyHtml:
The first time I felt that was when my daughter started preschool. We dropped her at 8 AM… and my wife and I sat in the McDonald’s next door until 12 noon waiting for school to end.

She walked in smiling. We were the emotional ones. She was ready. We weren’t.

This week, that feeling returned, in a bigger way.

My daughter is going on her first 4-day Outdoor Education trip to Big Bear. Her first time away from us for so long. She packed her own bag, made her own checklist, and ran to join her friends with full confidence.

And once again, my wife and I shared that quiet moment parents know so well, that mix of pride, nervousness, and the realization that your child is growing faster than you expected.

My wife felt it deeply too. She teaches our daughter things I don’t: how to take care of herself, how to stay thoughtful, how to stay organized. She even said, “She’s growing faster than I’m ready for.” And I could tell she was a little more nervous than our daughter, who was already laughing and chatting with her friends.

The school gave us option to write letters and we chose to write one for each night she’ll be away. I thought it would be simple… but when I actually sat down to write, everything shifted.

These letters made me think:

What do I really want her to learn? How do I guide her without making her feel like we’re missing her? How do I add meaning without adding emotional weight?

And that’s when I realized something important.

This trip isn’t just her milestone. It’s ours.

A chance for us, as parents, to practice the very values we want her to carry: confidence, curiosity, kindness, gratitude, responsibility, and the courage to try something new.

Because independence isn’t taught in one moment. It’s practiced in all the small moments when we trust our children to step forward and trust ourselves to step back.

She’ll return with stories, memories, and experiences that will shape her. And we’ll be here, growing alongside her.

Children grow fast. But sometimes, parenting asks us to grow even faster.

For the parents reading this what was the moment you felt your child growing up before you were ready?
subtitle: The Hardest Part of Parenting No One Talks About

title: Let Go
description: A quiet meditation on control, uncertainty and the strength it sometimes takes to release what can no longer be carried.
bodyHtml:
This comes from a place in me that knows what it feels like to carry things quietly.

Let It Go is my way of creating space, for anyone who’s ever felt overwhelmed, unseen, or simply needed a soft place to land.

Ever feel like your brain is full… but with nothing specific?

Like you're not sad, not angry...but not okay either.

That’s when we need to vent. Not for advice. Not to be fixed. Just to say things out loud, so they stop echoing inside.

But most of us don’t. We don’t want to burden others. We don’t want to sound dramatic. Or we just don’t have someone who gets it without judgment.

That’s why I started working on something called Ventit... a space where you can just be. Where no one interrupts you. No one tries to fix you. You speak, n just.. let it go... That’s it.

Because sometimes, feeling heard is all the healing we need.

And...If you ever need someone to listen, I’m here.

title: What Percy and Pluto Taught Me
description: For more than forty years, I never came close to a dog. Then our daughter asked for one, and Percy and Pluto quietly became two of my best teachers.
homeIntro: For more than forty years, I never came close to a dog. Then our daughter asked for one, and we came home with two.
atHeart: The things dogs teach you, presence, forgiveness, joy in small things, are the same things good relationships need, dressed up as a walk and a bowl of water.
bodyHtml:
For more than forty years, I had never really come close to a dog.

Then our daughter asked for one.

As often happens, the child asks, the parents agree, and the parents eventually become the ones doing most of the work.

We first went to see one puppy. But when we learned that he had a brother, we could not bring ourselves to separate them. We came home with both.

Pluto was a name we had always liked, and it continued the accidental tradition of names beginning with P in our family. Percy was inspired by Percy Jackson, which our daughter was reading at the time.

They came to us when they were not even eight weeks old.

Within two days, I was very close to giving them back.

It was overwhelming. The sleepless nights, the constant cleaning, the worry about whether we were doing everything correctly, it felt like we had taken on more than we could manage.

Fast forward two years, and Percy and Pluto are no longer pets. They are family.

I have always loved children, perhaps because of their innocence. They do not hold things in their hearts for long. They forgive quickly, move on easily and return with affection as though nothing happened.

Dogs seem to have the same gift.

They are excited every single time they see us. They find joy in the smallest things. They do not need grand plans to be happy. A walk, a familiar face, a few minutes of play or simply sitting beside us is enough.

When we lived in the United States, our travel plans gradually began revolving around them. Where could they come with us. Which hotel would allow them. How long could we be away. What would make the journey comfortable for them.

Yes, having dogs can make life more complicated.

People sometimes say that dogs restrict your freedom. You cannot travel as easily. You need to plan everything around them.

That is true.

But perhaps it is also a question of whether we see the glass as half full or half empty.

Even assuming we travel for thirty days a year, not having them may make those thirty days easier. I would rather think about the other 330 plus days, the warmth, joy, affection and kindness they bring into our home.

More importantly, what they quietly teach us during those days.

Our move from the United States back to Singapore was one of the hardest parts of this journey. The documentation, medical requirements, flights and constant anxiety about their safety made the relocation far more complicated.

But leaving them behind was never an option.

It was difficult. It was also completely worth it.

One day, I hope to write the longer story of their journey, or more accurately, our journey with them.

For now, the lessons are simple. Be excited to see the people you love. Live in the moment. Forgive quickly. Find joy in small things. Show loyalty through actions. Drink water. And never forget to play.

Percy and Pluto may have entered our home because our daughter wanted a dog.

But somewhere along the way, they became two of my best teachers.

For anyone raising a puppy, considering getting a dog, or moving with pets between the United States and Singapore, please feel free to reach out. We learned many things the hard way, and I would be happy to share what helped us.

title: Beyond Networking: What 20+ Teams and 100+ People Taught Me
description: The most meaningful relationships rarely began with an introduction. They were built while solving problems and doing meaningful work together.
bodyHtml:
A few weeks before graduation, I became curious.

How many different teams had I worked with during my UCLA Anderson journey?

I started counting.

Study groups.

Electives.

Competitions.

Consulting projects.

The podcast.

Cross-program collaborations.

Global immersion projects.

The final number surprised me.

By graduation, I had worked across more than 20+ teams and collaborated with over 100+ classmates, alumni, and community members.

If you had told me that on the first day of Leadership Foundations Week, I probably wouldn’t have believed you.

Not because the number is large.

Because at the time, I still considered myself someone most comfortable in familiar circles.

Looking back now, the number isn’t what matters.

What matters is what those teams taught me about leadership, collaboration, and people.

The First Lesson Started Outside the Classroom

One of the earliest experiences in the program was the ropes course during Leadership Foundations Week, We spent a day working through a series of team challenges.

Balancing a stick, Navigating ropes that became wider and more difficult as we moved forward.

Trust exercises that required partners to depend on one another.

And the challenge I remember most: climbing a tall pole and leaping forward to touch a hanging target that always seemed just a little farther away than expected.

I had participated in similar programs before.

Yet this one felt different.

Perhaps because I wasn’t just learning about teamwork.

I was learning something about myself.

I still remember some of my early interactions with classmates like Berj. Looking back, I was probably more focused on solving the problem than understanding the people around me. Like many leadership lessons, the learning came from realizing what I could have done differently.

The ropes course lasted only a day.

But in hindsight, it introduced a theme that would repeat throughout the next two years.

Every team would teach me something new.

Not just about business.

About people.

The Habit of Saying Yes

At first, I mostly stayed within the structure of the program.

Assigned study groups. Assigned projects. Assigned teams.

Then something changed. I joined an elective with people I had never worked with before. As someone who naturally leans toward being an introvert, this surprised me.

One of the turning points came during the AI Operations elective.

The class itself was fascinating and helped me better understand a field that is reshaping every industry. But what stayed with me most was the experience of working with a completely new team.

It would have been easy to stay within familiar circles.

Instead, new experience made it easier to say yes to the next one.

Then another project.

Then a competition.

Then a consulting engagement.

Then the podcast.

Then a cross-program collaboration.

What started as curiosity slowly became a habit.

And every new team exposed me to people who approached the world differently than I did.

Watching how different people approached the same challenge reminded me that the most valuable learning often comes from the people around you, not just the material being taught.

That realization stayed with me for the rest of the program.

Learning Through Different Lenses

As the program progressed, I found myself working with classmates from different industries, countries, functions, and professional backgrounds.

Some came from finance. Some from healthcare. Some from technology. Some from entrepreneurship. Others from government, consulting, nonprofits, and industries I knew very little about before UCLA.

One project might involve someone with deep financial expertise.

Another might include someone building or acquiring businesses in real time while we were learning the concepts in class.

In one study group, I experienced team dynamics that were very different from those I had known previously. The way people checked in on one another, celebrated milestones, and ensured everyone was included gave me a different perspective on teamwork and leadership.

Working with students from UCLA’s Full-Time MBA, FEMBA, Public Policy, Urban Planning, and other programs expanded that perspective even further.

The engineer sees a problem one way. The entrepreneur sees it another.

The policymaker sees something entirely different. None are necessarily right or wrong. They simply bring different lenses.

And leadership often begins with understanding those lenses.

Competitions Were Never About Winning

Somewhere along the way, I started participating in competitions.

The Ethics Challenge. The LMI Sand Prize. The HPE competition.

Looking back, I am grateful for the experiences and the recognition our teams received.

But the awards were never what made those experiences memorable.

What I remember are the discussions. The debates. The preparation.

The uncertainty.

The moments when a team had to decide which path to take despite incomplete information. Those experiences reinforced something I have observed throughout my career.

Pressure reveals character.

You learn who listens.

Who challenges assumptions respectfully.

Who builds consensus.

Who steps forward when leadership is needed.

Who quietly supports the team behind the scenes.

The trophies are nice.

The people are what stay with you.

Learning Beyond the Classroom

Not all learning happened in class projects or competitions.

One of the more unexpected experiences was helping build and support the UCLA EMBA podcast.

Working with Dylan, Salo, our hosts, guests, and the broader marketing team exposed me to a completely different form of collaboration.

Most teams are focused on solving problems. The podcast was focused on telling stories.

That required different skills.

Listening.

Curiosity.

Preparation.

Creating space for others to share their experiences.

It reminded me that collaboration is not always about execution.

Sometimes it is about helping others be heard.

Each experience added another layer to the learning.

What I Learned About Leadership

When people talk about the value of an MBA, they often talk about the network.

I’ve never been completely comfortable with that word.

Network can sound transactional.

As if the objective is to accumulate contacts.

That wasn’t my experience.

The relationships I value most were not built at networking events.

They were built while working through challenges together.

While preparing presentations.

While debating ideas.

While solving problems.

While occasionally disagreeing.

And while learning from one another.

Looking back, UCLA Anderson became a laboratory for understanding how different people think.

Every team taught me something.

Not just about business.

About perspective.

About leadership.

About myself.

A Final Reflection

When I started the program, I expected to learn from professors.

I did.

I expected to learn from coursework.

I did that too.

What I didn’t expect was how much I would learn simply by working with so many different people.

More than 20 teams.

More than 100 classmates, alumni, and collaborators.

Dozens of projects, conversations, presentations, competitions, and shared experiences.

Looking back, those numbers are not a measure of my network.

They are a reminder of how many opportunities I had to see the world through someone else’s eyes.

The projects will eventually become memories.

The presentations will be forgotten.

The competitions will come and go.

But the people, lessons, and perspectives I gained from working alongside them will stay with me for a very long time.

And that may be one of the most valuable lessons I take away from UCLA Anderson.
