title: Equality or Equity?
description: A ten-minute walk to school became a lesson in fairness, time and the wisdom that can come from the smallest voices.
bodyHtml:
Quick question.

Which is better, equality or equity?

Take a second and pick one.

A few mornings ago, my daughter asked me this while we were walking to school.

Lately life has been quite busy. Between work, the MBA, and everything that comes with building life away from the place we once called home, time feels like it moves very fast.

If I’m honest, one small regret during this MBA journey is that sometimes I feel I don’t spend enough time with my family.

So recently I started doing something simple.

Every morning I walk my daughter to school. It’s about a 10-minute walk, but it has quietly become the best part of my day. No phones, no rush. Just a little time to talk.

One morning she mentioned something interesting from school.

Equality vs. Equity.

So let me ask again.

Which do you think is better?

My first answer was equality.
Everyone gets the same thing. That sounded fair to me.

But my daughter shook her head.

“No,” she said. “Equity is better.”

I asked her why.

She paused for a moment and then said something that stayed with me.

“When it’s equal, it may not be fair.
And when it’s fair, it may not be equal.”

Then she explained it with a simple example.

Imagine a teacher giving the whole class granola bars.

Equality means every student gets the same granola bar.

But what if one student is allergic to nuts?
What if another skipped breakfast and is still hungry?
What if someone already ate?

Giving everyone the same thing looks fair.

But it doesn’t help everyone in the same way.

Equity means giving each student what they actually need.

I smiled because sometimes the most thoughtful ideas come from the smallest voices.

That morning reminded me of two things.

First, fairness is not always about treating everyone the same. Sometimes it is about understanding what people really need.

And second, in the middle of busy work, deadlines, and studying, the most important thing we can give our children is our time.

Sometimes all it takes is a 10-minute walk to school.

And sometimes during that walk, you realize your child might be the one teaching the lesson….

title: One Less Thing to Worry About
description: Customers may forget the presentation or the price. They remember whether your presence made a difficult moment easier.
bodyHtml:
Over the past few months, I’ve been reflecting on the beliefs that have quietly shaped how I work through customers, colleagues, leadership, and more than a few mistakes along the way.

Here’s one I’ve kept coming back to.

Early in my career, I thought customers remembered the best presentation.

Or the most competitive price.

Or even the project we delivered.

Like many people starting out, I assumed business was won in meeting rooms.

If we explained our solution well enough, submitted a competitive proposal, and delivered what we promised, that was success.

Over time, I realised that wasn’t what customers remembered.

What they remembered were the moments after the contract.

The unexpected phone call.

The missed deadline.

The design change.

The site issue.

The difficult conversation neither side wanted to have.

Those moments reveal far more about a relationship than the presentation ever did.

Winning a contract wasn’t the finish line.

It was simply the moment someone decided to trust us.

The real work started after the signatures.

Would we deliver?

Would we communicate honestly when something didn’t go according to plan?

Would we stay engaged long after the project was complete?

I don’t remember exactly when it happened, but somewhere along the way, one question quietly became my guide.

Can I become one less thing for my customer to worry about?

It sounds simple.

But it changed how I approached almost everything.

It meant taking ownership, even when the answer wasn’t immediately obvious.

It meant calling a customer before they had to call me.

It meant saying, “I don’t know yet, but I’ll find out,” instead of pretending to have all the answers.

It meant staying with a problem until it was resolved rather than until it was someone else’s responsibility.

Looking back, I don’t think customers expected perfection.

No project ever is.

What they wanted was confidence that someone cared as much about the outcome as they did.

Ironically, I think that’s what built the strongest relationships.

Not flawless execution.

Not perfect presentations.

Trust.

I’ve since realised this idea extends well beyond customers.

The best colleagues become one less thing for their teams to worry about.

The best leaders become one less thing for their people to worry about.

The best partners become one less thing for each other to worry about.

The context changes.

The principle doesn’t.

Customers may forget the presentation.

They may forget the proposal.

They may even forget parts of the project.

But they rarely forget how you made them feel when things became difficult.

More than twenty years into my career, that’s still a standard I try to hold myself to.

Not because I always achieve it.

But because I think it’s a goal worth coming back to.

A small note

Over the coming months, I’d like to write more about the beliefs that have quietly shaped how I work. Not because I think they’re universal, but because they’ve stood the test of experience for me.

I’d love to hear which beliefs have stayed with you throughout your own career.

title: The Editorial Page
description: How reading The Hindu with my grandfather taught me to look beyond what happened and ask what an argument was really trying to say.
bodyHtml:
I don’t remember when I started reading seriously.
But I remember who made me start.

Growing up in India, we subscribed to The Hindu. In our house, it wasn’t just a newspaper. It arrived every morning like something that had to be respected.

My grandfather would call me to sit next to him and read the headlines aloud. At first, it was about pronunciation. Difficult words. Long sentences. I would stumble. He would correct me patiently. Then he would turn to the editorial page.

“Read this,” he would say.

At that age, I didn’t know what an editorial meant. I assumed it was just another article. But I noticed something about the way he approached it. He listened differently. He would stop me midway and ask, “What do you think they are trying to say?”

Not what happened.
Not who said what.
But what they were trying to say.

I didn’t always have an answer.

Only later did I understand that he wasn’t just asking me to read. He was asking me to think.

An editorial forces you to follow an argument. It asks you to stay with a line of reasoning. To consider it fully before deciding whether you agree or disagree.

That habit, of staying with a thought long enough to understand it, stayed with me.

Over time, reading became something I associated with patience. Not effort. Not productivity. Just patience.

An article wasn’t something to get through. It was something to sit with.

Today, I still read. In fact, I probably read more than I did back then. But now, most of it happens on my phone.

News apps. Long-form essays. Analysis pieces. Links shared by friends. Headlines appearing between messages. The entire world fits in the palm of my hand.

And somewhere along the way, I began noticing a difference.

I finish an article and almost immediately move to the next one. A notification interrupts. Another headline pulls me in. A suggested link appears. Before I’ve fully formed a view, I’m already somewhere else.

It isn’t that I’ve stopped reading.

It’s that I don’t always linger.

And I sometimes wonder whether that lingering, that quiet pause after reading, was where most of the thinking actually happened.

Thinking, in other words, is not automatic. It is effortful.

And that effort matters. Research on deep reading suggests that when we follow complex arguments and wrestle with ambiguity, the brain strengthens the very networks responsible for comprehension, empathy, and reasoning. The struggle is not a side effect of thinking, it is part of how thinking develops.

Deliberate reasoning, holding competing ideas in mind, resisting quick judgment, staying with ambiguity, requires mental energy. But that energy builds capacity.

There is also research showing that frequent task-switching reduces depth of processing. When attention keeps shifting, information is encoded more shallowly. We recognize it, but we don’t always integrate it.

Maybe the shift isn’t that we’ve stopped reading.

Maybe we’ve just reduced the space between what we read and what we think.

When that space shrinks, I notice something subtle in myself. I react faster. I move on quicker. I form impressions before I’ve fully formed opinions. I skim arguments instead of sitting with them.

I don’t think this is about blaming phones. Phones are tools. They’ve made information more accessible than ever.

But they’ve also made switching effortless.

And when switching becomes effortless, lingering becomes intentional.

I find myself wondering what this means not just for us, but for children growing up in this environment.

If deep thinking requires effort, and effort is increasingly optional, what habits are forming?

If they mostly see adults swipe, scroll, and move on, are we modeling reflection or reaction?

The editorial page taught me that forming an opinion required patience. It required sitting with someone else’s reasoning before offering my own.

I’m not sure we’ve lost that ability.

But I do wonder whether we practice it less.

And increasingly, I think about another layer, the role of AI.

If reading shapes how we think, writing shapes it even more. Writing forces structure. It forces clarity. It forces you to wrestle with your own uncertainty. When tools begin assisting not just our search but our sentences, what happens to that cognitive effort?

I don’t have answers yet.

For now, I’m simply noticing the difference between how I learned to read and how I read today.

Maybe that quiet space after the editorial, the pause before speaking, mattered more than I realized.

I hope to explore more about what this means for children, and for how we write and think in an age where technology is becoming a collaborator in our words.

For now, I’m just trying to linger a little longer.

title: The Value of Being Bored
description: Boredom once felt like empty time. Looking back, it may have been the space where curiosity, reading and reflection quietly took root.
bodyHtml:
When did you last feel bored?

Not tired. Not distracted. Just bored. With nothing pulling at you and nowhere to be.

I find myself thinking about this more than I expected to.

· · ·

. . .

Growing up in India, I was bored all the time. There was not much to do. No real TV to speak of, no screens, no constant noise. So I would just sit. And at some point I found the big book rack in our home.

I became obsessed with the Atlas. Not for school, not for any reason really. I would just sit there turning pages, looking at countries, trying to read names I could not pronounce, wondering what those places looked like. Nobody told me to. It just happened, because there was nothing else going on.

Around that same time I started writing a diary. First I would write it for my grandfather, then I kept going on my own. That habit stayed with me for years. I never sat down and decided to become someone who keeps a diary. It just grew out of all that quiet time.

Back then I thought being bored was something to get through. Looking back, I think it was something that was actually building me.

· · ·

I came across a video on YouTube recently. Arthur Brooks, a professor at Harvard, made it for Harvard Business Review. The title was simple: You Need to Be Bored. Here’s Why.

Brooks talks about something called the default mode network. It sounds technical but the idea is simple. When your mind has nothing to focus on, it does not switch off. It switches over. It starts to wander. And in that wandering, something happens. You start thinking about bigger things. Questions you never get to during a busy day. Things that matter to you but never quite rise to the surface.

He makes a point that stayed with me. Every time we feel even slightly bored and reach for our phone, we are cutting that process off. We never let the mind get there. And over time, without that space, something starts to feel hollow. We stay busy but we lose the thread of what we are actually doing it all for.

What struck me was not the research. It was the recognition. I had been feeling this for a while without having a word for it.

· · ·

These days the closest I get to that childhood boredom is my drive between Irvine and UCLA. Sometimes it is an hour. Sometimes two. And I almost always turn everything off.

No music. No podcast. No calls.

Just the road and whatever is in my head.

What happens in that time is hard to explain. My thoughts just run. Like a movie that plays on its own. Things I have not had time to think about come up. Ideas connect in ways they do not when I am busy. Sometimes something useful comes out of it. Not because I was trying to solve anything. Just because I gave it room.

That drive is probably the only real idle time I have now. And I protect it.

· · ·

A few years ago when my daughter was four, we put her into a Montessori school in Singapore. The school had one condition. Screen time had to come down to two hours a day.

We knew we were guilty. The TV had become the easy option. It kept her occupied so we could get on with things.

We agreed to the condition. And then we realised it was not just about removing the screen. We had to fill that time with something. So we gave her our time. We started reading to her. Slowly she started picking up books on her own.

She loves reading now. I watch her sometimes just sitting quietly with a book, completely in her own world. That did not come from us pushing her. It came from giving her space and then filling it with the right thing.

We gave her boredom back. And she did the rest herself.

· · ·

I think about kids growing up today. Every quiet moment gets filled before they even notice it is there. A screen appears, something starts playing, the moment is gone. They never get the chance to just sit and not know what to do with themselves.

And I wonder what that means. Not in a dramatic way. Just quietly. What thoughts are not forming? What habits are not growing? What questions are never being asked, because there is never enough silence to ask them?

I am not saying phones are bad. I use mine constantly. But I do think we have all quietly stopped giving ourselves the one thing that used to come naturally.

Space to just be.

In my last piece I wrote about lingering. About how we have stopped pausing after we read something, stopped letting it settle before moving to the next thing. Boredom feels like the bigger version of that same idea. Not a pause after something. Just empty time. Time with no purpose, no input, no plan.

The Atlas did not teach me geography. The diary did not teach me to write. The silence did.

I do not have a solution to offer. I am just noticing something. And I wanted to ask you the same question I have been asking myself.

When did you last let yourself be bored?

I want to keep thinking about what this means for children, and also what happens as AI starts doing more of our thinking and writing for us. More on that soon.

If you missed the first piece

Lingering: on reading, attention, and the space between words and thought

References

Arthur Brooks, You Need to Be Bored. Here’s Why (Harvard Business Review, YouTube)

Maryanne Wolf, Reader Come Home

Arthur Brooks, The Happiness Files

Research on the default mode network: Marcus Raichle, Washington University

title: Am I Using AI to Extend My Thinking, or Avoid It?
description: Every powerful tool changes what we practise. The real question is what happens when convenience begins to replace the struggle that develops judgement.
bodyHtml:
My mom used to say: “Anything in excess is poison.” I didn’t think much of it when I was younger. But over time, I started noticing something. I used to remember phone numbers. I used to do quick mental math. I used to sit with problems longer before reaching for help. Then smartphones arrived. They didn’t make me less intelligent. They simply removed the need to practice those small habits. Now I see a similar shift happening again. At a workshop recently, a speaker said something that stayed with me: “Generative AI optimizes for the statistical average.” Whether taken literally or not, the idea made me pause. Because LLMs are incredibly powerful. They can retrieve, summarize, connect, and generate at a speed no human can match. But every powerful tool changes what we practice. Calculators changed arithmetic. GPS changed navigation. Search engines changed memorization.

So the question becomes: What will LLMs change in us? The more I use them, the more I notice a subtle shift. I reach for answers faster than I sit with questions. I sometimes generate before I think through the problem. And it makes me ask myself: Am I using AI to extend my thinking… or to avoid it? Because the value was never just the answer. It was the struggle required to reach it. I don’t worry about AI becoming smarter than me. I worry about becoming too dependent on something that isn’t thinking at all.
homeIntro: Every powerful tool changes what we practise. The real risk isn't AI outsmarting us, it's leaning on it until we stop thinking for ourselves.
atHeart: Every powerful tool changes what we practise, and the real risk isn't AI outsmarting us, it's leaning on it so much that we stop thinking for ourselves.

title: When AI Makes Everything Faster, What Still Makes It Matter?
description: AI can accelerate execution, but speed cannot replace human judgement, emotional timing or authentic connection.
bodyHtml:
AI is being celebrated for making advertising faster and cheaper.

But speed was never the hard part.

The harder question is whether we’re using AI to strengthen authentic human connection or quietly replacing it.

Because people don’t connect with how efficiently something was produced. They connect with what feels real.

I recently listened to a podcast on AI in advertising, using Coca-Cola as an example.

The case was compelling. AI can reduce production time, lower costs, and allow brands to test and scale creative faster than ever before.

All of that is true.

But advertising has never been a production problem. It has always been a connection problem .

The speed story

AI adoption in advertising is accelerating quickly.

Nearly half of advertisers plan to use AI for media strategy in the near term, and most marketers already using AI cite speed as the primary benefit, faster creation, faster iteration, faster decisions.

Speed is no longer rare. It’s becoming expected.

The performance story

There’s also evidence that AI-assisted campaigns can improve short-term performance. Better targeting, faster testing, and automated optimization can drive measurable gains.

Graph caption: Performance gains don’t automatically translate to connection.

AI improves efficiency inside the system . It does not decide what should matter to people.

The connection story

This is where the picture becomes more nuanced.

Consumer research suggests that most people feel neutral about AI-generated ads. Only a small percentage say it improves how they feel about a brand. Many describe these ads as forgettable or emotionally flat.

Indifference rarely shows up immediately in metrics. But over time, it quietly erodes trust and brand equity.

What this really means

Coca-Cola didn’t become iconic because its ads were produced efficiently. It became iconic because its messages consistently reflected human moments , joy, nostalgia, togetherness, belonging.

AI can help execute those ideas faster and cheaper. It cannot originate why they matter.

In fact, AI is doing something else very effectively.

It is exposing weak thinking faster .

Shallow ideas now get produced at scale. Authentic ideas get amplified, if they exist in the first place.

My take

As AI enters every field, speed and efficiency will increasingly look the same everywhere.

What won’t is judgment .

AI excels at execution, generating options, testing variations, optimizing outcomes. But it doesn’t sense cultural undercurrents, emotional timing, or when less is more.

That still requires people who stay close to real conversations, real behaviors, and real moments.

The advantage won’t come from choosing between humans or AI. It will come from knowing what must stay human , and using AI to support it, not substitute it.

AI is like a camera with perfect resolution. It still needs someone who knows what’s worth capturing.

AI will continue to reshape how work gets done.

The harder leadership task is deciding what should not be automated , even when it could be.

Because brands aren’t remembered for how efficiently something was produced, they’re remembered for how they made people feel.

Where are you drawing that line in your organization?

Figures shown are directional, based on aggregated industry research (eMarketer, NielsenIQ, Zappi, SurveyMonkey).

Grateful for the strategy discussions in class that helped shape this perspective - Professor Jana Gallus

title: When Awareness Isn’t Enough
description: Data can show us what we are doing. Change often begins only when we understand why we are doing it.
bodyHtml:
I used to think I had a healthy relationship with my phone. A few scrolls between meetings, maybe a video before bed, nothing major.

Then, in my Happiness class, we were asked to track how we spend our time. I thought it’d be quick, a few numbers, maybe a chart.

Instead, it showed me something uncomfortable: Every 30 minutes or so, I was spending about five minutes scrolling. By day’s end, nearly two hours gone .

Apple’s Screen Time confirmed it. But the data didn’t change my habits. Awareness alone wasn’t enough.

That’s when I decided to dig deeper.

Apple’s reports looked neat, but vague. Four hours on my phone… doing what exactly? Learning or doom-scrolling?

I set daily limits. Then hit “Ignore for today” , every single day.

One day scroll too many. That’s when I realized. I didn’t lack data. I lacked meaning.

So, each time I picked up my phone, I wrote why , scrolling, learning, listening, or just passing time.

Within days, patterns appeared. I wasn’t tracking time anymore, I was tracking intent. And that shift changed everything.

👉 Awareness tells you what you’re doing.

👉 Meaning tells you why you’re doing it. That’s when real change begins.

Now, when I reach for my phone, I pause, not to judge, but to ask, why now? That small question keeps me honest.

If Apple ever asked for feedback, I’d tell them: Don’t just show hours. Show purpose. Help people reflect on how that time feels.

Because data informs. But meaning transforms.

title: Are We Really Eating Food, or Additives?
description: Using the Yuka app to scan groceries revealed how much of what we buy is closer to chemistry than food, and what that means for the planet.
bodyHtml:
At home, we've always tried to eat healthy, mostly thanks to my wife, who keeps us on track. But honestly, I never realized how much of what we eat isn't real food until I started using the Yuka app.

What surprised me most weren't the calories or sugar, but the additives. According to The Guardian, ultra-processed foods now make up 70% of what's sold in grocery stores and more than half of the calories we consume.

That number made me pause. We may be shopping for food, but most of what we're buying is chemistry.

One detail from the article blew my mind: making a common chocolate additive from soybean oil requires steps like degumming in a hot reactor, chemically isolating phospholipids, and decolorization using hydrogen peroxide. And a common sweetener starts off as corn steeped in acid, then broken down using enzymes and acids, and recrystallized. That's what goes into something that ends up in my mouth.

And when you think about the energy, chemicals, and global transport behind every ingredient, it's easy to see how our food choices link directly to emissions and the environment.

For me, Yuka has been a real eye-opener. I now scan products just to understand what's actually inside, and it's changed how I look at everyday food.

Sometimes awareness begins with a quiet scan, and a louder wow.

title: My First Gamble, and the Slap That Taught Me About Money
description: A childhood lottery win in India, and the one sharp lesson that shaped how I've thought about easy money ever since.
bodyHtml:
Everyone talks about their first win. I still remember my first loss, even though I actually won.

At work recently, we were talking about vacations. Someone mentioned Vegas, slot machines, free drinks, the whole setup designed to keep you playing. That reminded me of my first "gamble," back in 3rd grade in India.

Those colorful one-rupee lottery boards were everywhere. Out of curiosity, I bought one. To my surprise, I won fifteen rupees. Overjoyed, I ran home to show my dad my big win. His reaction? One sharp slap.

That was the first and last time I ever gambled for money. And though it stung, the lesson stayed with me: never chase easy money, respect what you earn.

Years later, when I moved to Singapore, I learned that citizens and permanent residents must pay an entry levy just to enter a casino, a quiet nudge reminding people that luck has a cost.

Funny how a small slap can teach a lifelong lesson about money and mindset. What's the earliest money lesson you still remember?

title: Not Everything That Shines Is Meant to Be Chased
description: A moment from the Ramayana, and what a golden deer can teach us about mistaking urgency for importance.
bodyHtml:
With all the chatter around AI, tech, innovation and disruption, it's easy to get carried away. Some days it feels like everything is urgent and everything needs our attention right now. But sometimes an old story explains things better.

In the Ramayana, there is a moment where a simple illusion quietly changes the direction of the entire journey. And it begins not with a fight, but with a golden deer.

Rama, Sita and Lakshmana were living a calm and peaceful life in the forest. One morning, Sita noticed a deer that looked unlike anything they had ever seen. Its body shone like gold. Sita wished to have it. Rama didn't see anything wrong, maybe it would make her smile. So he walked into the forest to bring it back. The deer kept moving ahead, always close enough to chase, but never close enough to catch.

Back at the hut, Lakshmana felt a strange stillness. Something didn't seem right, but he couldn't explain why. Eventually, the golden glow disappeared, and with it came a cry that changed everything. Only later did they learn the truth, it wasn't a deer at all. It was Maricha, a demon wearing beauty like a mask.

One small distraction. One moment of "this looks special." And the entire story shifted.

I think about that sometimes. Not everything that shines is meant to be chased. And not everything that feels urgent is truly important. Before running toward the next glittering thing, it helps to pause for a moment and ask: what am I chasing, and why?

title: What Will a Ten-Year-Old Actually Remember?
description: Speaking at Career Week, and choosing small truths over job titles: a bee, a water drop, and a shy boy on a school stage.
bodyHtml:
A big thank you to Caitlin Maxwell for giving me the opportunity to speak at Career Week. While preparing, I kept asking myself one simple question: what will a ten-year-old actually remember? Not job titles. Not responsibilities.

I didn't want to lecture them about careers. I spoke the way I do with my own daughter, like a friend sharing small stories that helped me along the way. A story. A feeling. A small idea they can quietly carry for years.

So I built the session around the tiny truths that shaped me: the bee, a tiny creature working all day to create one spoon of honey, a reminder that small steps, done with heart, add up. The water drop and the rock, showing how consistency, not intensity, shapes the strongest things in nature. My school skit moment, a shy boy hiding behind taller classmates until a teacher called my name, five seconds that changed everything.

In between those stories, we spoke about something deeper: the importance of gratitude, caring for people, and caring for the planet. Whether it's remembering the people who help us grow or respecting the planet that holds all of us together, kids understood this faster than we imagine.

We closed with my favorite reminder, life lessons from a dog, because sometimes the greatest teachers walk on four legs: live in the moment, run and play daily, drink water and rest, let go quickly, be curious.

If the session sparked even one tiny thought in a young mind, that's good enough. Small steps, toward a big future.

title: Sixteen Months In, I Realized It Was Never Just the Degree
description: From an awkward first meeting at Topgolf to a village built through study groups, finance quarters, and late nights, an MBA reflection sixteen months in.
bodyHtml:
They say an MBA is about the degree. It is not. Sixteen months in, I've realized it's about something else entirely.

It started before classes even kicked off, meeting at Topgolf. A little awkward, a little excited, not knowing those faces would soon become familiar names across multiple WhatsApp groups. Somewhere along the way, "quick chats" stopped being quick.

Then came the first study groups, tailgates, long class weekends and even longer nights, a finance quarter that tested sleep, patience, and optimism, and forming capstone teams, realizing we're in the final stretch.

Luskin became our regular meeting spot, not just for class, but for check-ins, catch-ups, and conversations that went beyond the agenda. One finance lesson that will stay with me: aim for "high alpha, low beta", focus on what you can truly control, and don't let the noise throw you off course.

But beyond the academics, something deeper happened. We grew, personally, not just professionally. Friendships formed that don't feel time-bound, the kind where you check if a classmate is nearby when you travel, or reach out just to catch up, not because you need help, but because you care.

Someone once said it takes a village. Somehow, we built one. A village you can return to, for support, laughter, or simply to feel understood.

Sixteen months in, I know it was never just about the degree. It was about the village we built and the one we carry forward.

title: This Year, I Realized I Wasn't the Listener I Thought I Was
description: An introvert's reflection on the difference between observing people and truly listening to them.
bodyHtml:
This is the time of year when everything gets wrapped for us. I wanted to do something quieter. I wanted to unwrap my year.

The feeling reminded me of opening an old book, when you catch the faint fragrance of dried petals pressed between its pages. Something familiar. Something you'd forgotten was there.

I'm an introvert. I observe. I notice patterns. And for a long time, I assumed that made me a good listener. This year, I realized I wasn't. I was also a fast judge.

Through a mix of classes and long, one-on-one conversations, I started digging a little deeper, both into myself and into the people around me. When you sit with someone for that long, the cover comes off. You hear about detours and quiet resilience that never makes it into a bio.

Preparation for those conversations stopped being about clever questions or answers. It became about giving the conversation room to breathe. I noticed myself pausing more, listening longer, letting people finish the thought I thought I already understood.

To make sense of it all, I went back to writing. Not for an audience, but for myself. I'm still an introvert. I'm just learning to leave more space. I'll let that keep unfolding.

title: The Squirrel and the Bridge
description: Bridges don't fail where the biggest rocks are placed. They fail where the small gaps are ignored.
bodyHtml:
Armies are moving massive stones. The vision is bold. The structure is ambitious. In the middle of all this, a small squirrel keeps carrying tiny pebbles, one at a time. Ever wondered what the squirrel is doing here?

I used to open my presentations with this image. I'd tell them: you're doing the hard, visible work, designing complex systems. I'm not here to redesign the bridge or challenge the vision. I'm here to focus on the gaps.

Because bridges don't fail where the biggest rocks are placed. They fail where the small gaps are ignored. Those gaps look minor, until stress hits, until compliance is tested, until what looked right on paper meets the reality of the field.

In high-stakes environments, this mindset isn't optional. It's the difference between a system that appears strong and one that actually holds.

I've chosen to do the work that protects what others build. To strengthen systems before they're tested. One pebble at a time.

Do you focus on the big rocks, or the gaps?

title: Sometimes, Being Present Is the Point
description: At my daughter's DARE graduation, a lesson about how peer pressure never really disappears, we just rename it as adults.
bodyHtml:
It was my daughter's DARE graduation day at school. Like I try to do with most of her school events, I made sure I was there, not for an outcome, but simply to show up as a friend and say: I'm here to see you complete this.

Learning early about peer pressure, choices, and influence is important, and honestly, lessons many adults could still benefit from. As she explained her project on good and bad influencers, I was surprised by how deeply she had thought about it. That's when it struck me that peer pressure doesn't disappear when we grow up, we just rename it. In adults, it becomes culture, career pressure, or "this is how it's always been done."

Neither of us knew the projects would be evaluated, or that some would be recognized. When hers was awarded Best Cinema, it came as a surprise to both of us. But what stayed with me wasn't the recognition. It was how humbling the moment felt.

What I found most gratifying was seeing her talk about these ideas openly and without fear. Sometimes, being present isn't about applause or results, it's about showing up so someone knows they mattered even before the outcome. And sometimes, just by being there, you end up learning something yourself.

title: How Are the Butterflies Doing?
description: A UCLA sustainability elective, a conservationist's simple recurring question, and what it taught me about caring for something small and fragile.
bodyHtml:
I didn't expect my sustainability elective to leave me emotional. I'm currently taking an elective called Leaders in Sustainability at UCLA, offered through UCLA Environment and taught by Professor Travis Longcore.

What stood out immediately is that Professor Longcore isn't just teaching from books. He has spent years working in the real world, in conservation, in cities, and with communities that are often ignored. You can feel that experience in the way he speaks.

He shared a story about Arthur Bonner, someone he knew personally and worked closely with on a conservation project protecting a rare butterfly species, work that was featured in a National Geographic documentary. Professor Longcore shared that every time he spoke to Arthur, Arthur would always ask the same question: "How are the butterflies doing?"

That question kept coming back to me. There was something powerful about it, how caring for something small and fragile, and watching new life grow, left a lifelong mark on him.

It made me think differently about sustainability. It's not only about policies, reports, or big systems. Sometimes, sustainability is about connection, about purpose, about how caring for life outside ourselves can slowly change who we are. That moment in class was emotional and grounding. It reminded me that leadership in sustainability isn't abstract. It's human.

title: Culture Survives Because People Choose to Live It
description: On Lunar New Year, the world's largest human migration, and a lesson from WD-40's founder on what separates culture from strategy.
bodyHtml:
Wishing everyone celebrating a very Happy Lunar New Year. Each year, this season triggers Chunyun, the largest human migration in the world. In 2026 alone, nearly 9.5 billion passenger trips are expected over 40 days as millions travel home despite cost, crowds, and inconvenience.

That always makes me pause. People don't endure that for logistics. They do it because it matters. Across Asia, whether in Chinese or Indian traditions, festivals aren't just holidays. They carry forward identity and shared values. The same pattern exists in organizations.

In class, Professor John Ullmen shared Garry Ridge's perspective from the WD-40 Company: culture is values and behaviors, practiced consistently, backed by the will of people to live them. Strategy is outcomes.

At WD-40, that shows up clearly. Employees are called "tribe members." Leaders coach instead of command. Mistakes become learning moments. Repeated. Consistent. Modeled from the top. That's how culture compounds.

Whether in society or in organizations, culture survives because people choose to live it, especially when it's inconvenient. Every organization has a culture. The only question is whether it's by design or by default.
homeIntro: Watching Lunar New Year travel and a lesson from WD-40's founder, I realised culture survives only when people choose, consistently, to live it.
atHeart: Culture isn't a policy. It survives only when people choose, consistently, to live it, especially when it's inconvenient.

title: Sustainability Isn't a Project You Finish
description: What UCLA's own power plant, underground tunnels, and native landscaping taught me about dreaming at the scale of decades.
bodyHtml:
There's a quote I once heard: "If you reach all your dreams in this lifetime, you probably didn't dream big enough." Every time I hear leaders in sustainability speak, that thought comes back to me.

Listening to Nurit Katz talk about UCLA's work, I realized something. This isn't about small fixes. It's about dreaming at the scale of decades.

Did you know there are miles of underground tunnels carrying steam and chilled water across campus every single day? UCLA runs its own power plant, and captures waste heat to heat and cool buildings. The campus can disconnect from the grid and keep a hospital running during a blackout. Electric buses are being tested to charge while driving, through coils embedded under a campus road.

And then there's the part that really stayed with me. It's not just energy. It's ecology. Rethinking landscaping to use native plants. Reducing certain pesticides because they harm owls higher up the food chain. Paying attention to pollinators. That level of detail surprised me.

Not just big infrastructure decisions, but small, thoughtful choices that ripple through an ecosystem. Sustainability isn't a project you finish. It's long-term thinking. It's building systems someone else will inherit and improve. Maybe that's what dreaming big really looks like.

title: Understanding People Is Harder Than We Think
description: A simple point from a David Brooks piece: most of us don't really take time to understand others. We react fast and move on.
bodyHtml:
Understanding people is harder than we think. I came across a piece by David Brooks. His point is very simple: most of us don't really take time to understand others. We react fast, form an opinion, and move on.

But real understanding takes something else. You need to slow down. You need to pay attention. You need to let the other person finish. Not every conversation needs advice. Not every moment needs a response. Sometimes, just giving someone space to speak is enough.

Sounds simple. Most of the time, the simplest things are the toughest to do, because we overlook them. This connects with my philosophy: the easiest way to connect with someone is to give them space first, then listen. Many are going through a lot. Most are just looking for that space, and someone who will listen.

title: The Real Risk Isn't Being Wrong. It's Assuming the Game Stops Moving
description: Walking into rooms at UCLA where I wasn't the expert taught me more than any framework did.
bodyHtml:
Here's a fascinating truth in sports: the moment you think you've mastered the game is often the moment you start falling behind. Not because your performance drops, but because the baseline of excellence keeps moving forward.

That idea has stayed with me. After many years in industry, I came to UCLA Anderson expecting most of my learning to come from new frameworks and tools. Instead, some of the most meaningful growth has come from deliberately walking into rooms where I wasn't the most familiar with the subject.

Over the past two years, I've worked alongside medical, law, and public policy students across sustainability initiatives, non-profit consulting projects and much more. What stood out wasn't just the difference in how people think, but how openly they shared what they knew, while remaining equally curious about perspectives outside their own field. That combination is rare, and powerful.

John Wooden said success is the peace of mind that comes from knowing you gave your absolute best. That idea is liberating. It removes the pressure of always needing to have all the answers, and replaces it with something more valuable: curiosity.

In the long run, the real risk isn't being wrong. It's assuming the game stops moving.

title: The 40 Year Leader vs. the 130 Year Giant: A Real Market Play
description: A market leader went from 25% to nearly 70% share in five years. Then a 130 year old global giant decided to enter the same market.
bodyHtml:
In one of the world's fastest growing economies, I watched something remarkable unfold. A 40 year old market leader in the FMCD sector went from around 25% share to nearly 70% in just five years. And then came the twist: a 130 year old global giant, a household name in a complementary category, decided to enter the same market.

This wasn't theory. It was a real life scenario I faced, and it changed the way I think about competition, perception, and execution.

The market context. The FMCD category here is unusual. Nearly half the market remains unorganized, but as the middle class expands, more customers are shifting to organized players. That migration creates massive opportunity, but also sharpens the competition among the few labels that dominate the organized side.

The market leader's playbook. The leader's rise from challenger to dominant force came down to three moves. Exclusivity over discounts: rather than being everywhere, they limited availability to select stores, and retailers were forbidden from offering discounts. Speed as a differentiator: they promised delivery in 2 to 4 hours, when the rest of the market operated on timelines of weeks. Dealer incentives that mattered: margins were only part of the story, dealers were motivated through cash prizes and rewards tied to volumes.

The entrant. Then came the 130 year old global giant. On paper, it looked formidable: global reputation, deep pockets, strong household recognition. But its operating model was not designed for this market. Lead times stretched four to eight weeks, dealer margins were slightly lower, a centralized decision-making process slowed execution, and there were no local plants yet.

The dilemma. How does a nimble market leader defend against a giant with global muscle? And how does the giant overcome its slower, more rigid model to break into a market where speed and exclusivity already define success? It is a David versus Goliath battle, except David already holds the crown.

My reflection. Being close to this scenario showed me that competition isn't just about better products or bigger budgets. It is about aligning how customers perceive value, how quickly you deliver on promises, and how motivated your partners feel to champion your label. The leader did not win by cutting prices. They won by owning the perception of quality and reliability, and delivering consistently.

This was a real life scenario, and it reminded me that strategy is rarely about a single right answer. It is about structuring choices, aligning execution, and staying consistent over time.

title: Holding the Stretch
description: A yoga practice in Singapore becomes a quiet lesson in staying with discomfort, in the body and in the mind.
bodyHtml:
Since coming back to Singapore, I've been slowly restarting some of my old routines.

One of them is yoga.

I've noticed there is a choice in almost every stretch. I can do what's comfortable, or I can push myself that little bit further.

No one really knows the difference except me.

But pushing further isn't necessarily the hardest part. Holding the pose for those extra few seconds is.

Those last five counts somehow feel much longer than the first five. Your body wants you to release. You know you can.

And then you try to stay.

The other day, while holding a pose, something I had written recently came back to me.

Lingering.

I had been thinking about how quickly we move from one thing to another today, and whether we're giving ourselves enough time to sit with a thought before moving on.

Yoga suddenly made me see that a little differently.

Stretching the body is one thing. Staying in the stretch is another.

Perhaps the mind works that way too.

We can expose ourselves to new ideas, different arguments, things that challenge what we believe. But maybe the real work happens in what comes next.

Can I stay with an uncomfortable thought without immediately dismissing it?

Can I hold the uncertainty without reaching for an answer?

When I keep doing this with the body for a few days, something changes. A stretch that was difficult starts becoming easier. The body seems to create a little more space.

I wonder if the mind works that way too.

One idea from a Public Policy class at UCLA has stayed with me: learning to hold multiple complex truths at the same time.

I like that idea because holding two truths doesn't mean we never form a view. It means we give ourselves enough space to understand the tension between them before we do.

Perhaps the mind needs that space too.

With the body, we call it holding the pose.

With the mind, perhaps it's lingering.

I'm finding I need to practice both.

title: When Answers Become Easy, What Happens to Thinking?
subtitle: What friction used to force us to do.
description: AI is making answers easier to get. I’m beginning to wonder what else the effort of getting to an answer was doing for us.
bodyHtml:
I’ve been thinking about something as AI makes answers easier to get.

For most of my career, getting to an answer took effort.

You searched for information.
You spoke to people.
You compared views.
Sometimes you worked with incomplete information and had to make sense of it yourself.

That effort was not always efficient.

But I wonder if it was doing something else for us too.

It forced us to think.

Today, AI can give me analysis, alternatives and possible answers in seconds.

That is incredibly useful.

But when we remove so much of the effort involved in getting to an answer, do we also remove some of the thinking that used to happen along the way?

I’ve started noticing this even in my own use of AI.

An answer appears quickly. It sounds reasonable. And it is very easy to move on.

But perhaps that is exactly when I need to slow down.

Do I agree with it?

What is it missing?

Is this even the right question?

And more importantly, is this something worth doing in the first place?

We have spent years trying to make information easier to access.

AI may take that much further.

That is progress.

But maybe one of the things we will have to learn is how to preserve some of the thinking that friction used to force upon us.

Not because the old way was better.

But because judgment still needs to come from somewhere.

title: Participation Is Not Belonging
subtitle: What culture looks like when people feel safe enough to disagree.
description: A reflection on participation, psychological safety, and what it really means to belong at work.
bodyHtml:
I used to think team-building events were a sign of a strong culture.

I’m less sure now.

I have seen workplaces where the signs of community were everywhere.

Offsites.

Celebrations.

Photographs on the wall.

Plenty of language about being “one team.”

People participated in all of it.

But participation is not the same as belonging.

One test of belonging, at least for me, is much simpler:

Can people speak honestly?

Can someone say:

“I disagree.”

“I don’t think this will work.”

“The customer is telling us something different.”

And say it without worrying that speaking up will come back to hurt them?

Because silence can easily be mistaken for agreement.

Sometimes people are silent because they agree.

Sometimes they are silent because they have learned that disagreeing is not worth the risk.

That difference matters.

Not just for culture.

For the business too.

No one person sees everything.

The people closest to customers see things leadership may not.

The people executing the work see problems others may miss.

The whole point of having a team is to bring those views into the room before decisions are made.

Otherwise, you can have many people in an organization and still end up with only one person’s thinking.

That is why I have started looking at culture differently.

Not by how many people attend the offsite.

Not by how many photographs are on the wall.

But by what happens in the room when someone disagrees.

You can bring people together.

You can get them to participate.

But if they don’t feel safe enough to disagree, that is participation.

Not belonging.
